arXiv:1509.05120v1 [math.CA] 17 Sep 2015

Normalized incomplete beta function: log-concavity in parameters and other properties

D.B. Karp Note: E-mail: D. Karp – dimkrp@gmail.com Affiliation:   Far Eastern Federal University, 8 Sukhanova street, Vladivostok, 690950, Russia Affiliation:   Institute of Applied Mathematics, FEBRAS, 7 Radio Street, Vladivostok, 690041, Russia

Abstract. The normalized incomplete beta function can be defined either as cumulative distribution function of beta density or as the Gauss hypergeometric function with one of the upper parameters equal to unity. Logarithmic concavity/convexity of this function in parameters was established by Finner and Roters in 1997. Their proof is indirect and rather difficult; it is based on generalized reproductive property of certain more general distributions. These authors remark that these results ”seems to be very hard to obtain by usual analytic methods”. In the first part of this paper we provide such proof based on standard tools of analysis. In the second part we go one step further and investigate the sign of generalized Turán determinants formed by shifts of the normalized incomplete beta function. Under some additional restrictions we demonstrate that these coefficients are of the same sign. We further conjecture that such restrictions can be removed without altering the results. Our method of proof also leads to various companion results which may be of independent interest. In particular, we establish linearization formulas and two-sided bounds for the above mentioned Turán determinants. Further, we find two combinatorial style identities for finite sums which we believe to be new.

Keywords: Incomplete beta function, Gauss hypergeometric function, log-concavity, combinatorial identity

MSC2010: 33B20, 33C05, 05A19

1. Motivation and introduction.

The beta distribution is perhaps the single most important continuous compactly supported probability distributions. Its particular cases include the Wigner semicircle, the Marchenko-Pastur and the arcsine laws; it is important in Bayesian analysis as conjugate prior to binomial and geometric distributions [8]; it plays a role in a large number of applications ranging from population genetics to project management. The beta distribution is defined by the density xa−1​(1−x)b−1/B⁡(a,b)x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/B(a,b) supported on [0,1][0,1], where B⁡(a,b)B(a,b) is Euler’s beta function [3]. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the beta density is given by the normalized incomplete beta function

Ix​(a,b)=Bx​(a,b)B⁡(a,b)=∫0xta−1​(1−t)b−1​𝑑t∫01ta−1​(1−t)b−1​𝑑t.I_{x}(a,b)=\frac{B_{x}(a,b)}{B(a,b)}=\frac{\int_{0}^{x}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt}{\int_{0}^{1}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}dt}.

In a recent paper [4] containing the mathematical analysis supporting a recent investigation related to lottery frauds in Florida, the authors solve the following optimization problem

∑imci​αi→min⁡under constraint​f​(α1,α2,…,αm)=∏i=1mIpi​(wi,αi−wi+1)≥ε.\sum_{i}^{m}c_{i}\alpha_{i}\to\min~~\text{under constraint}~f(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{m}I_{p_{i}}(w_{i},\alpha_{i}-w_{i}+1)\geq\varepsilon.

For efficient numerical solution of such problem it is desirable that the function ff be quasi-concave which implies that the feasible set of the problem is convex and local minimizer is also global. Since monotonic transformations do not alter quasi-concavity it suffices then to show that log⁡f\log{f} is a concave function. This fact, in turn, is implied by log-concavity of b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} on (0,∞)(0,\infty). The purpose of this paper is to investigate the log-concavity/convexity properties of the function Ix​(a,b)I_{x}(a,b) viewed as the function of parameters aa and bb. In particular, we demonstrate that b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} is indeed log-concave on (0,∞)(0,\infty), while a→Ix​(a,b)a\to{I_{x}(a,b)} is log-convex on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for b∈(0,1)b\in(0,1) and log-concave for b>1b>1. Log-concavity of b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} is equivalent to the positivity of the generalized Turán determinant

Ix​(a,b+α)​Ix​(a,b+β)−Ix​(a,b)​Ix​(a,b+α+β)I_{x}(a,b+\alpha)I_{x}(a,b+\beta)-I_{x}(a,b)I_{x}(a,b+\alpha+\beta)

for all α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, while log-convexity (log-concavity) of a→Ix​(a,b)a\to{I_{x}(a,b)} is equivalent to negativity (positivity) of

Ix​(a+α,b)​Ix​(a+β,b)−Ix​(a,b)​Ix​(a+α+β,b).I_{x}(a+\alpha,b)I_{x}(a+\beta,b)-I_{x}(a,b)I_{x}(a+\alpha+\beta,b).

We go one step further and study the signs of the power series coefficients (in powers of xx) of the above Turán determinants. Under some additional restrictions we demonstrate that these coefficients are of the same sign. We further conjecture that such restrictions can be removed without altering the results. Our method of proof also leads to various companion results which may be of independent interest. In particular, we establish linearization formulas and two-sided bounds for the above Turán determinants. Further, we find two combinatorial style identities for finite sums which we believe to be new.

When this paper was nearly completed we discovered that log-concavity/convexity of the CDF of beta distribution has been demonstrated in 1997 by Finner and Roters in their fundamental work [7]. Partial results in this direction have been previously given by the same authors in [6] and by Das Gupta and Sarkar in [9]. However, their log-concavity proofs are very involved and indirect - they appear as a by-product of generalized reproductive property of certain probability measures. Finner and Roters note in their paper that ”we are now able to conclude a result for the Beta distribution which seems to be very hard to obtain by usual analytic methods”. The proofs presented in this paper are precisely ”by usual analytic methods”. The power series coefficients of the Turán determinants have not been considered by the above authors, so our results in this direction strengthen the achievements of [7].

We conclude the introduction by presenting an alternative expression for the normalized incomplete beta function in terms of the Gauss hypergeometric function [3]

F12​(α,β,γ,z)=∑n=0∞(α)n​(β)n(γ)n​n!​zn.{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\alpha,\beta;\gamma;z)=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\alpha)_{n}(\beta)_{n}}{(\gamma)_{n}n!}z^{n}.

Indeed, using Euler-Pochhammer integral representation

F12​(α,β,γ,x)=Γ⁡(γ)Γ⁡(β)​Γ​(γ−β)​∫01uβ−1​(1−u)γ−β−1​(1−u​x)−α​𝑑u{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\alpha,\beta;\gamma;x)=\frac{\Gamma(\gamma)}{\Gamma(\beta)\Gamma(\gamma-\beta)}\int_{0}^{1}u^{\beta-1}(1-u)^{\gamma-\beta-1}(1-ux)^{-\alpha}du

we get by a change of variable and application of Euler’s formula B⁡(a,b)=Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)/Γ⁡(a+b)B(a,b)=\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b):

Ix​(a,b)=Γ⁡(a+b)​xaΓ⁡(a+1)​Γ​(b)​F12​(1−b,a,a+1,x).I_{x}(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a+b)x^{a}}{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(b)}{{}_{2}F_{1}}(1-b,a;a+1;x).

Further, applying another Euler’s formula

F12​(α,β,γ,x)=(1−x)γ−α−β​F12​(γ−α,γ−β,γ,x){{}_{2}F_{1}}(\alpha,\beta;\gamma;x)=(1-x)^{\gamma-\alpha-\beta}{{}_{2}F_{1}}(\gamma-\alpha,\gamma-\beta;\gamma;x)

we obtain the well-known representation

Ix​(a,b)=Γ⁡(a+b)​xaΓ⁡(a+1)​Γ​(b)​(1−x)b​F12​(a+b,1,a+1,x)=xa​(1−x)b​∑n=0∞Γ⁡(a+b+n)Γ⁡(b)​Γ​(a+1+n)​xn.I_{x}(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a+b)x^{a}}{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(b)}(1-x)^{b}{{}_{2}F_{1}}(a+b,1;a+1;x)=x^{a}(1-x)^{b}\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(a+b+n)}{\Gamma(b)\Gamma(a+1+n)}x^{n}. (1)

2. Log-concavity of Ix​(a,b)I_{x}(a,b) in aa and bb.

The proof of the next theorem has been inspired by the log-concavity proof for incomplete gamma function given in [1]. See a related result in [2].

  Theorem 1

For each fixed a>0a>0 and x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) the function b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} is strictly log-concave on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

∂2∂b2​log⁡(B⁡(a,b))=ψ′​(b)−ψ′​(a+b)>0,\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial{b}^{2}}\log(B(a,b))=\psi^{\prime}(b)-\psi^{\prime}(a+b)>0, (2)

where ψ⁡(z)=Γ′​(z)/Γ⁡(z)\psi(z)=\Gamma^{\prime}(z)/\Gamma(z) is logarithmic derivative of the gamma function and the inequality follows from the fact that z→ψ′​(z)z\to\psi^{\prime}(z) is decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) according to the representation

ψ′​(z)=∑n=0∞1(n+z)2.\psi^{\prime}(z)=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n+z)^{2}}.

Further,

Bx​(a,b)2​∂2∂b2​log⁡(Ix​(a,b))=Bx​(a,b)​∫0xta−1​(1−t)b−1​[log⁡(1−t)]2​dt−[∫0xta−1​(1−t)b−1​log⁡(1−t)​dt]2−Bx​(a,b)2​(ψ′​(b)−ψ′​(a+b))=:Ua,b​(x)B_{x}(a,b)^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial{b}^{2}}\log(I_{x}(a,b))=B_{x}(a,b)\int_{0}^{x}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}[\log(1-t)]^{2}dt-\\ \left[\int_{0}^{x}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\log(1-t)dt\right]^{2}-B_{x}(a,b)^{2}(\psi^{\prime}(b)-\psi^{\prime}(a+b))=:U_{a,b}(x)

We have Ua,b​(0)=Ua,b​(1)=0U_{a,b}(0)=U_{a,b}(1)=0. The second equality can be seen by setting x=1x=1 and then differentiating which is legitimate by continuous double differentiability or by setting x=1x=1 in the above formula and computing the integrals. We aim to demonstrate that Ua,b​(x)U_{a,b}(x) is decreasing on (0,x1)(0,x_{1}) and increasing on (x1,1)(x_{1},1) for some x1∈(0,1)x_{1}\in(0,1). This will prove that Ua,b​(x)<0U_{a,b}(x)<0 for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) for each a,b>0a,b>0. We have

Va,b​(x):=Ua,b′​(x)xa−1​(1−x)b−1=∫0xta−1​(1−t)b−1​[log⁡(1−t)]2​dt+Bx​(a,b)​[log⁡(1−x)]2−2log(1−x)∫0xta−1(1−t)b−1log(1−t)dt−2Bx(a,b)(ψ′(b)−ψ′(a+b)).V_{a,b}(x):=\frac{U_{a,b}^{\prime}(x)}{x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}}=\int_{0}^{x}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}[\log(1-t)]^{2}dt+B_{x}(a,b)[\log(1-x)]^{2}\\ -2\log(1-x)\int_{0}^{x}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\log(1-t)dt-2B_{x}(a,b)(\psi^{\prime}(b)-\psi^{\prime}(a+b)).

Definition of Ix​(a,b)I_{x}(a,b) immediately leads to the reflection formula

Ix​(a,b)=1−I1−x​(b,a).I_{x}(a,b)=1-I_{1-x}(b,a).

This implies

∂2∂a2​log⁡(Ix​(a,b))=[Ix​(a,b)]−2​{I1−x​(b,a)​∂2∂a2​I1−x​(b,a)−[∂∂a​I1−x​(b,a)]2}−[Ix​(a,b)]−2​∂2∂a2​I1−x​(b,a).\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial{a}^{2}}\log(I_{x}(a,b))=[I_{x}(a,b)]^{-2}\biggl\{I_{1-x}(b,a)\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial{a}^{2}}I_{1-x}(b,a)-\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial{a}}I_{1-x}(b,a)\right]^{2}\biggr\}\\ -[I_{x}(a,b)]^{-2}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial{a}^{2}}I_{1-x}(b,a).

The first term is negative according to Theorem 1. The second term, however, may change sign depending on the values of bb and xx as demonstrated by numerical evidence. Hence, we cannot draw any definitive conclusion about log-concavity of a→Ix​(a,b)a\to{I_{x}(a,b)} from the reflection formula. Indeed, it turns out that the result depends on the value of bb. Nevertheless, a method similar to that used in the proof of Theorem 1 also works here combined with the following lemma.

  Lemma 1

For fixed α>0\alpha>0 define fα​(x):(0,∞)→(−∞,∞)f_{\alpha}(x):(0,\infty)\to(-\infty,\infty) by

fα​(x)=(ψ⁡(x+α)−ψ⁡(x))2+ψ′​(x+α)−ψ′​(x).f_{\alpha}(x)=(\psi(x+\alpha)-\psi(x))^{2}+\psi^{\prime}(x+\alpha)-\psi^{\prime}(x).

Then fα​(x)<0f_{\alpha}(x)<0 if 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and fα​(x)>0f_{\alpha}(x)>0 if α>1\alpha>1.

Proof. Using recurrence relations ψ⁡(x+1)=ψ⁡(x)+1/x\psi(x+1)=\psi(x)+1/x and ψ⁡(x+1)=ψ⁡(x)−1/x2\psi(x+1)=\psi(x)-1/x^{2}, we calculate

f⁡(x+1)−f⁡(x)=(ψ⁡(x+α+1)−ψ⁡(x+1))2−(ψ⁡(x+α)−ψ⁡(x))2+ψ′​(x+α+1)−ψ′​(x+α)+ψ′​(x)−ψ′​(x+1)=(ψ⁡(x+α+1)−ψ⁡(x+1)+ψ⁡(x+α)−ψ⁡(x))​(ψ⁡(x+α+1)−ψ⁡(x+1)−ψ⁡(x+α)+ψ⁡(x))+1x2−1(x+α)2=(2​ψ​(x+α)+1x+α−2​ψ​(x)−1x)​(1x+α−1x)+1x2−1(x+α)2=αx⁡(x+α)​(2​ψ​(x)−2​ψ​(x+α)+αx⁡(x+α))+α⁡(2​x+α)x2​(x+α)2=2​αx⁡(x+α)​(ψ⁡(x)−ψ⁡(x+α)+1x).f(x+1)-f(x)=\\ (\psi(x+\alpha+1)-\psi(x+1))^{2}-(\psi(x+\alpha)-\psi(x))^{2}+\psi^{\prime}(x+\alpha+1)-\psi^{\prime}(x+\alpha)+\psi^{\prime}(x)-\psi^{\prime}(x+1)\\ =(\psi(x+\alpha+1)-\psi(x+1)+\psi(x+\alpha)-\psi(x))(\psi(x+\alpha+1)-\psi(x+1)-\psi(x+\alpha)+\psi(x))\\ +\frac{1}{x^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+\alpha)^{2}}=\left(2\psi(x+\alpha)+\frac{1}{x+\alpha}-2\psi(x)-\frac{1}{x}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x+\alpha}-\frac{1}{x}\right)+\frac{1}{x^{2}}-\frac{1}{(x+\alpha)^{2}}\\ =\frac{\alpha}{x(x+\alpha)}\left(2\psi(x)-2\psi(x+\alpha)+\frac{\alpha}{x(x+\alpha)}\right)+\frac{\alpha(2x+\alpha)}{x^{2}(x+\alpha)^{2}}\\ =\frac{2\alpha}{x(x+\alpha)}\left(\psi(x)-\psi(x+\alpha)+\frac{1}{x}\right).

Writing gα​(x)g_{\alpha}(x) for the function in parentheses and utilizing the integral representations

  Theorem 2

Suppose x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) is fixed. Then:

3. Coefficient-wise log-concavity of Ix​(a,b)I_{x}(a,b).

As mentioned in the introduction, logarithmic concavity of b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} demonstrated in Theorem 1 is equivalent to the inequality

ϕa,b,α,β​(x):=Ix​(a,b+α)​Ix​(a,b+β)−Ix​(a,b)​Ix​(a,b+α+β)>0\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x):=I_{x}(a,b+\alpha)I_{x}(a,b+\beta)-I_{x}(a,b)I_{x}(a,b+\alpha+\beta)>0 (3)

valid for all positive values of aa, bb, α\alpha and β\beta and each x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1). This inequality expresses the strict Wright log-concavity of b→Ix​(a,b)b\to{I_{x}(a,b)} - a property equivalent to log-concavity for all continuous functions [14, Chapter I.4], [15, Section 1.1]. On the other hand, formula (1) implies that the function of ϕa,b,α,β​(x)\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x) defined in (3) has the power series expansion

ϕa,b,α,β​(x)=x2​a​(1−x)2​b+α+β​∑k=0∞ϕk​xk.\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x)=x^{2a}(1-x)^{2b+\alpha+\beta}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}\phi_{k}x^{k}. (4)

It is then natural to ask whether and when the coefficients ϕk\phi_{k} are positive. In general, for a given formal power series

f⁡(μ,x)=∑k=0∞fk​(μ)​xkf(\mu;x)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}f_{k}(\mu)x^{k} (5)

with nonnegative coefficients fk​(μ)f_{k}(\mu) which depend continuously on a parameter μ\mu from a real interval II, we will say that μ→f⁡(μ,x)\mu\to{f(\mu;x)} is coefficient-wise Wright log-concave on II for α∈A⊆[0,∞)\alpha\in{A}\subseteq[0,\infty), β∈B⊆[0,∞)\beta\in{B}\subseteq[0,\infty) if the formal power series for the product difference

f⁡(μ+α,x)​f​(μ+β,x)−f⁡(μ,x)​f​(μ+α+β,x)f(\mu+\alpha;x)f(\mu+\beta;x)-f(\mu;x)f(\mu+\alpha+\beta;x)

has nonnegative coefficients at all powers of xx for α∈A\alpha\in{A}, β∈B\beta\in{B} and all μ∈I\mu\in{I}. If coefficients are strictly positive we say that the corresponding property holds strictly. If coefficients are non-positive we talk about coefficient-wise Wright log-convexity. These concepts using slightly different terminology were introduced by the author (jointly with S.I. Kalmykov) in [10].

Conclusions of Theorem 2 can be restated in terms of the function

ψa,b,α,β​(x):=Ix​(a+α,b)​Ix​(a+β,b)−Ix​(a,b)​Ix​(a+α+β,b)=x2​a+α+β​(1−x)2​b​∑k=0∞ψk​xk\psi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x):=I_{x}(a+\alpha,b)I_{x}(a+\beta,b)-I_{x}(a,b)I_{x}(a+\alpha+\beta,b)=x^{2a+\alpha+\beta}(1-x)^{2b}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}\psi_{k}x^{k} (6)

as follows: if a>0a>0 and 0<x<10<x<1 then ψa,b,α,β​(x)<0\psi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x)<0 for 0<b<10<b<1 and ψa,b,α,β​(x)>0\psi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x)>0 for b>1b>1. Just like with ϕa,b,α,β​(x)\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}(x) it is then natural to consider the coefficient-wise log-convexity and log-concavity of a→x−a​(1−x)−b​Ix​(a,b)a\to x^{-a}(1-x)^{-b}I_{x}(a,b), i.e. study the sign of the coefficients ψk\psi_{k}.

The main purpose of this section is to give partial solution to the following conjectures representing substantial strengthenings of Theorems 1 and 2, respectively.

  Conjecture 1

The coefficients ϕk\phi_{k} are positive for all a,b,α,β>0a,b,\alpha,\beta>0 and x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), so that b→x−a​(1−x)−b​Ix​(a,b)b\to x^{-a}(1-x)^{-b}I_{x}(a,b) is strictly coefficient-wise Wright log-concave on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for these values of parameters.

  Conjecture 2

The coefficients ψk\psi_{k} are negative for all a,α,β>0a,\alpha,\beta>0 and x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) if 0<b<10<b<1 and positive if b>1b>1, so that a→x−a​(1−x)−b​Ix​(a,b)a\to x^{-a}(1-x)^{-b}I_{x}(a,b) is strictly coefficient-wise Wright log-convex on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) and 0<b<10<b<1; and a→x−a​(1−x)−b​Ix​(a,b)a\to x^{-a}(1-x)^{-b}I_{x}(a,b) is strictly coefficient-wise Wright log-concave on (0,∞)(0,\infty) for α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1) and b>1b>1.

Our approach also leads to a number of related results which may be of independent interest. These include alternative formulas for the coefficients ϕk\phi_{k} and ψk\psi_{k}, linearization identities for the product differences of hypergeometric functions, two-sided inequalities for the Turán determinants formed by normalized incomplete beta functions and two presumably new combinatorial identities.

We will need the following lemma (see [10, Lemma 3]).

Suppose μ→f⁡(μ,x)\mu\to{f(\mu;x)} is coefficient-wise Wright log-concave on [0,∞)[0,\infty) for α=1\alpha=1, β≥0\beta\geq 0, i.e.

f⁡(μ+1,x)​f​(μ+β,x)−f⁡(μ,x)​f​(μ+β+1,x)f(\mu+1;x)f(\mu+\beta;x)-f(\mu;x)f(\mu+\beta+1;x)

(7)

Proof. First we investigate the function ψa,b,1,μ​(x)\psi_{a,b,1,\mu}(x) defined in (6). Using (1) we compute

demonstrated in [11, p.72]. Next we set g⁡(a)=Ix​(a,b)/xa​(1−x)bg(a)=I_{x}(a,b)/x^{a}(1-x)^{b} and calculate

The next corollary refines Theorem 2 and gives partial solution to Conjecture 2.

This corollary can also be derived from our previous results in [10, Theorem 3] and [11, Theorem 2], however, the above derivation has the advantage of presenting the explicit formulas for the coefficients ψk\psi_{k} which do not follow from these references.

ϕa,b,1,βx2​a​(1−x)2​b+1+β=a​Γ​(a+b)​Γ​(a+b+β)Γ⁡(b+1)​Γ​(b+β+1)​Γ​(a+1)2​∑m=0∞(a+b+β)m+1−(a+b)m+1(a+1)m​xm=a​Γ​(a+b)​Γ​(a+b+β)Γ⁡(b+1)​Γ​(b+β+1)​Γ​(a+1)2{(a+b+β)2F1(1,a+b+β+1a+1;x)−(a+b)2F1(1,a+b+1a+1;x)}.\frac{\phi_{a,b,1,\beta}}{x^{2a}(1-x)^{2b+1+\beta}}=\frac{a\Gamma(a+b)\Gamma(a+b+\beta)}{\Gamma(b+1)\Gamma(b+\beta+1)\Gamma(a+1)^{2}}\sum\limits_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a+b+\beta)_{m+1}-(a+b)_{m+1}}{(a+1)_{m}}x^{m}\\ =\frac{a\Gamma(a+b)\Gamma(a+b+\beta)}{\Gamma(b+1)\Gamma(b+\beta+1)\Gamma(a+1)^{2}}\left\{(a+b+\beta){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,a+b+\beta+1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right)\right.\\ \left.-(a+b){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,a+b+1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right)\right\}. (12)

Next denote f⁡(b)=Ix​(a,b)/xa​(1−x)bf(b)=I_{x}(a,b)/x^{a}(1-x)^{b}. For α∈ℕ\alpha\in\mathbb{N} we have

ϕa,b,α,βx2​a​(1−x)2​b+α+β=f(b+α)f(b+β)−f(b)f(b+α+β)=[f(b+α)f(b+β)−f(b+α−1)f(b+β+1)]+[f(b+α−1)f(b+β+1)−f(b+α−2)f(b+β+2)]+⋯+[f⁡(b+2)​f​(b+β+α−2)−f⁡(b+1)​f​(b+β+α−1)]+[f⁡(b+1)​f​(b+β+α−1)−f⁡(b)​f​(b+β+α)].\frac{\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta}}{x^{2a}(1-x)^{2b+\alpha+\beta}}=f(b+\alpha)f(b+\beta)-f(b)f(b+\alpha+\beta)=[f(b+\alpha)f(b+\beta)\\ -f(b+\alpha-1)f(b+\beta+1)]+[f(b+\alpha-1)f(b+\beta+1)-f(b+\alpha-2)f(b+\beta+2)]+\cdots\\ +[f(b+2)f(b+\beta+\alpha-2)-f(b+1)f(b+\beta+\alpha-1)]+[f(b+1)f(b+\beta+\alpha-1)-f(b)f(b+\beta+\alpha)].

Each expression in brackets has the form x−2​a​(1−x)−2​b−α−β​ϕa,b+α−j,1,β−α+2​j−1x^{-2a}(1-x)^{-2b-\alpha-\beta}\phi_{a,b+\alpha-j,1,\beta-\alpha+2j-1}, j=1,2,…,αj=1,2,\ldots,\alpha. Hence, we can apply formula (12) to each such bracket which yields (11). □\hfill\square

The next corollary refines Theorem 1 and gives partial solution to Conjecture 1.

  Corollary 4

Suppose α∈ℕ\alpha\in\mathbb{N}. Then the coefficients ϕk\phi_{k} defined in (4) can be computed by

ϕk=∑j=0α−1a​Γ​(a+b+j)​Γ​(a+b+β+α−j−1)[Γ⁡(a+1)]2​Γ​(b+j+1)​Γ​(b+β+α−j)​(a+1)k×{(a+b+β+α−j−1)k+1−(a+b+j)k+1}.\phi_{k}=\sum\limits_{j=0}^{\alpha-1}\frac{a\Gamma(a+b+j)\Gamma(a+b+\beta+\alpha-j-1)}{[\Gamma(a+1)]^{2}\Gamma(b+j+1)\Gamma(b+\beta+\alpha-j)(a+1)_{k}}\times\\ \left\{(a+b+\beta+\alpha-j-1)_{k+1}-(a+b+j)_{k+1}\right\}. (13)

If, furthermore, β≥α−1\beta\geq\alpha-1 and β>0\beta>0 then ϕk>0\phi_{k}>0.

Proof. Formula (13) follows immediately from (11). According to Lemma 2 for β≥α−1\beta\geq\alpha-1 the sign of ϕk=ϕk​(α,β)\phi_{k}=\phi_{k}(\alpha,\beta) is determined by the sign of ϕk​(1,β)\phi_{k}(1,\beta). In view of (12) for α=1\alpha=1 we have

ϕk​(1,β)=a​Γ​(a+b)​Γ​(a+b+β)Γ⁡(b+1)​Γ​(b+β+1)​Γ​(a+1)2​(a+1)k​((a+b+β)k+1−(a+b)k+1),\phi_{k}(1,\beta)=\frac{a\Gamma(a+b)\Gamma(a+b+\beta)}{\Gamma(b+1)\Gamma(b+\beta+1)\Gamma(a+1)^{2}(a+1)_{k}}((a+b+\beta)_{k+1}-(a+b)_{k+1}),

which is clearly positive for β>0\beta>0. □\hfill\square

Remark. Substituting (1) for IxI_{x} into the definition of ϕa,b,α,β\phi_{a,b,\alpha,\beta} given in (3) and changing notation we can rewrite (11) as the following linearization identity for the quadratic form in Gauss hypergeometric functions

(a+b)n+1(b)n+1​F12​(a+b+n+1,1a+1,x)​F12​(a+b+β,1a+1,x)−(a+b+β)n+1(b+β)n+1​F12​(a+b,1a+1,x)​F12​(a+b+β+n+1,1a+1,x)=ab⁡(b+β)∑j=0n(a+b)j​(a+b+β)n−j(b+1)j​(b+β+1)n−j×{(a+b+β+n−j)​F12​(a+b+β+n+1−j,1a+1,x)−(a+b+j)​F12​(a+b+j+1,1a+1,x)}.\frac{(a+b)_{n+1}}{(b)_{n+1}}{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b+n+1,1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b+\beta,1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right)\\ -\frac{(a+b+\beta)_{n+1}}{(b+\beta)_{n+1}}{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b,1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b+\beta+n+1,1\\ a+1\end{array};x\!\right)\\ =\frac{a}{b(b+\beta)}\sum\limits_{j=0}^{n}\frac{(a+b)_{j}(a+b+\beta)_{n-j}}{(b+1)_{j}(b+\beta+1)_{n-j}}\times\\ \left\{\!(a+b+\beta+n-j){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b+\beta+n+1-j,1\\ a+1\end{array}\!\!;x\!\right)\!-\!(a+b+j){{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}a+b+j+1,1\\ a+1\end{array}\!\!;x\!\right)\!\right\}. (14)

Here n=α−1n=\alpha-1 is any nonnegative integer, while other parameters as well as xx can be arbitrary complex by analytic continuation. In particular, when n=0n=0 the above identity after some rearrangement reduces to

aa−c+1​F12​(1,a+1c,x)​[F12​(1,bc,x)+c−1b−c+1]=bb−c+1​F12​(1,b+1c,x)​[F12​(1,ac,x)+c−1a−c+1].\frac{a}{a-c+1}{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,a+1\\ c\end{array};x\!\right)\left[{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,b\\ c\end{array};x\!\right)+\frac{c-1}{b-c+1}\right]\\ =\frac{b}{b-c+1}{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,b+1\\ c\end{array};x\!\right)\left[{{}_{2}F_{1}}\!\!\left(\!\!\begin{array}[]{l}1,a\\ c\end{array};x\!\right)+\frac{c-1}{a-c+1}\right].

Formula (14) leads to a curious combinatorial identity which is presumably new.

  Corollary 5

For arbitrary nonnegative integers mm, nn the following identity holds

ab⁡(b+β)​∑j=0n(a+b)j​(a+b+β)n−j(b+1)j​(b+1+β)n−j​{(a+b+β+n−j)m+1−(a+b+j)m+1}=(a+1)m​∑k=0m(a+b)k​(a+b+β)m−k(a+1)k​(a+1)m−k​{(a+b+k)n+1(b)n+1−(a+b+β+m−k)n+1(b+β)n+1}.\frac{a}{b(b+\beta)}\sum\limits_{j=0}^{n}\frac{(a+b)_{j}(a+b+\beta)_{n-j}}{(b+1)_{j}(b+1+\beta)_{n-j}}\{(a+b+\beta+n-j)_{m+1}-(a+b+j)_{m+1}\}\\ =(a+1)_{m}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{m}\frac{(a+b)_{k}(a+b+\beta)_{m-k}}{(a+1)_{k}(a+1)_{m-k}}\left\{\frac{(a+b+k)_{n+1}}{(b)_{n+1}}-\frac{(a+b+\beta+m-k)_{n+1}}{(b+\beta)_{n+1}}\right\}.

Proof. The claimed identity follows on equating coefficients at xmx^{m} on both sides of the (14) and using the formula (μ+n+1)k​(μ)n+1=(μ)k​(μ+k)n+1(\mu+n+1)_{k}(\mu)_{n+1}=(\mu)_{k}(\mu+k)_{n+1}. □\hfill\square

The next corollary presents two-sided bounds for the Turán determinant formed by shifts of Ix​(a,b)I_{x}(a,b) in the second parameter.

  Corollary 6

Suppose ν\nu is a positive integer b>νb>\nu, a>0a>0. Then

m​x2​a​(1−x)2​b≤[Ix​(a,b)]2−Ix​(a,b+ν)​Ix​(a,b−ν)≤M​[Ix​(a,b)]2mx^{2a}(1-x)^{2b}\leq[I_{x}(a,b)]^{2}-I_{x}(a,b+\nu)I_{x}(a,b-\nu)\leq M[I_{x}(a,b)]^{2} (15)

for all x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1). Here

m=[Γ⁡(a+b)]2[Γ⁡(a+1)]2​[Γ⁡(b)]2−Γ⁡(a+b−ν)​Γ​(a+b+ν)[Γ⁡(a+1)]2​Γ​(b−ν)​Γ​(b+ν),M=(b)ν​(a+b−ν)ν−(a+b)ν​(b−ν)ν(b)ν​(a+b−ν)ν.\begin{split}&m=\frac{[\Gamma(a+b)]^{2}}{[\Gamma(a+1)]^{2}[\Gamma(b)]^{2}}-\frac{\Gamma(a+b-\nu)\Gamma(a+b+\nu)}{[\Gamma(a+1)]^{2}\Gamma(b-\nu)\Gamma(b+\nu)},\\[5.0pt] &M=\frac{(b)_{\nu}(a+b-\nu)_{\nu}-(a+b)_{\nu}(b-\nu)_{\nu}}{(b)_{\nu}(a+b-\nu)_{\nu}}.\end{split}

Proof. Inequality from below is just a rewriting of the inequality ϕa,b−ν,ν,ν≥x2​a​(1−x)2​b​ϕ0\phi_{a,b-\nu,\nu,\nu}\geq{x^{2a}(1-x)^{2b}}\phi_{0} which follows from nonnegativity of the coefficients ϕk\phi_{k} for all k=0,1,…k=0,1,\ldots To prove the upper bound consider the function

b→F⁡(b)=Ix​(a,b)​Γ​(b)xa​(1−x)b​Γ​(a+b)=∑n=0∞(a+b)nΓ⁡(a+n+1)​xn=∑n=0∞(a+b)n​n!Γ⁡(a+n+1)​xnn!.b\to F(b)=\frac{I_{x}(a,b)\Gamma(b)}{x^{a}(1-x)^{b}\Gamma(a+b)}=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a+b)_{n}}{\Gamma(a+n+1)}x^{n}=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a+b)_{n}n!}{\Gamma(a+n+1)}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}.

It is easy to check that the coefficients {n!/Γ⁡(a+n+1)}n=0∞\{n!/\Gamma(a+n+1)\}_{n=0}^{\infty} form a log-convex sequence. Then according to [12, Theorem 1] the above function is log-convex, so that for b>νb>\nu we have F⁡(b−ν)​F​(b+ν)≥[F⁡(b)]2F(b-\nu)F(b+\nu)\geq[F(b)]^{2}. This inequality can be rewritten as

Ix​(a,b−ν)​Ix​(a,b+ν)≥[Γ⁡(b)]2​Γ​(a+b+ν)​Γ​(a+b−ν)[Γ⁡(a+b)]2​Γ​(b+ν)​Γ​(b−ν)​[Ix​(a,b)]2.I_{x}(a,b-\nu)I_{x}(a,b+\nu)\geq\frac{[\Gamma(b)]^{2}\Gamma(a+b+\nu)\Gamma(a+b-\nu)}{[\Gamma(a+b)]^{2}\Gamma(b+\nu)\Gamma(b-\nu)}[I_{x}(a,b)]^{2}.

Simple rearrangement of the above inequality gives the upper bound in (15). □\hfill\square
